title: py-sdk-stream-ack-model-and-composed-signal-extensions
creator: Ava Chen
description: Problem: Developers integrating long-running streaming chat completions struggle to build reliable resume/retry logic and non-blocking event handling. Current Python SDK provides raw event streams but leaves complex signal composition (ACK/HEARTBEAT/CANCEL) and idempotent reconciliation to each user. This ticket designs and implements an SDK-level acknowledgement model plus composable control signals and deferred event hooks to make common retry and resume patterns ergonomic and safe for production apps.
motivation: Reduce customer implementation bugs, reduce support tickets for 'lost partial responses' and 'duplicate messages' during retries/failover. Provide a compact API that enables idempotent resumes, bounded memory callback handling, and clear backpressure semantics so applications can safely integrate streaming chat into event-driven architectures.
proposed_solutions: A - Minimal: expose low-level control signals (ACK/HEARTBEAT/CANCEL) and docs with recipes. Leaves reconciliation to users.
B - Middleware: provide a small middleware layer that manages a monotonic ack token, exposes a resume_token to clients, and offers an on_event callback queue with size limits.

C - High-level: introduce ChatStreamManager that handles leases, checkpoint persistence helpers, automatic idempotent deduping of emitted messages, and out-of-the-box retry policies (with backoff and token reuse).
decision: Choose B with opt-in extensions from C. We implement a lightweight middleware (ChatStreamAck) that maintains an ack counter and exposes a stable resume_token API. Additionally ship a companion 'deferred_hook' utility that runs user callbacks on a worker thread pool with configurable concurrency and soft queue limits. Keep full ChatStreamManager as a follow-up to avoid API bloat in 2.7.0.
chosen_solution_rationale: B provides the best tradeoff for short release cycle: it reduces user burden while staying small. It avoids a heavy stateful manager in the SDK that would require more lifecycle surface area (persistence adapters, migration). The deferred hooks solve the common blocking-callback issue immediately.
api_examples:
# Basic usage: receive events and ack progress
from redwood import ChatClient
client = ChatClient(api_key=...)
stream = client.chat.stream(messages, ack_mode="lease")
# stream yields Event objects with .type, .seq, .payload, .resume_token
for ev in stream:
    if ev.type == "message":
        process(ev.payload)
        stream.ack(ev.seq)
    elif ev.type == "end":
        stream.ack_all()
        break

# Deferred hooks: run user handlers without blocking stream reading
from redwood.sdk.streaming import deferred_hook
@deferred_hook(max_workers=4, queue_limit=256)
def save_to_db(ev):
    db.write(ev.payload)
# register hook on stream
stream.on("message", save_to_db)
acceptance_criteria: SDK exposes a ChatStream object with ack(seq), ack_all(), and resume_token attributes
Deferred hook helper available with max_workers and queue_limit; unit tests cover backpressure behavior when queue_limit is exceeded
End-to-end test: simulated server restart causes client to resume using persisted resume_token and not duplicate acknowledged messages (dedupe tolerance validated with integration test harness)
API docs and quickstart snippet added to docs site under "Streaming ergonomics"
Bench: no more than 8% p95 CPU overhead for streaming in the Python SDK compared to baseline (without deferred hooks) at 100 concurrent streams on a developer laptop profile
implementation_notes: Design will introduce a small internal ring buffer for ack metadata (seq -> acked boolean + timestamp) with eviction policy after ack. The resume_token is a compact base64 blob containing last_ack_seq and a short checksum; serverside is backward compatible with empty token. Deferred hooks use concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor with soft queue implemented via queue.Queue and reject policy that triggers an on_drop callback.
compatibility_considerations: Defaults maintain current behavior: ack_mode defaults to 'manual' (no ack tracking). Enabling ack_mode="lease" is opt-in. Resume tokens are optional; clients without tokens continue to work. The server will accept token-less resumes with weaker guarantees (may replay last chunk) — documented.

risks_and_mitigations: Risk: Users misunderstand ack semantics and double-ack leading to negative dedupe side effects. Mitigation: explicit docs, API names ack(seq)/ack_all(), and a warning log when double-ack detected.

Risk: Deferred hooks cause silent data loss when queue is full. Mitigation: default on_drop behavior is to call registered on_drop callback (user can persist to fallback) and emit telemetry metric; also surface an explicit exception API for critical handlers.
Risk: Resume token leakage (sensitive info). Mitigation: token is minimal and opaque; add recommendation to store tokens in customer-managed vaults and mark token as ephemeral in docs.
Risk: Performance regression. Mitigation: add benchmark microtests and opt-out knobs (deferred_hook disabled by default).
